status_summary: The modernization strand is underway through appropriations rather than the structural changes the Mandate lists. Congress provided $12.5 billion in Public Law 119-21, signed 2025-07-04 (Sec. 40003; DOT calls it the Working Families Tax Cut Act), for a new air traffic control system that DOT announced on 2025-05-08 and says will be deployed by the end of 2028. On 2026-09-28 Senator Eric Schmitt introduced the Modern Skies Act as S. 5572, a $30.1 billion second phase referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and endorsed by DOT and the FAA Administrator; DOT's FY2027 budget request (released 2026-04-03) asks $4.0 billion for FAA Facilities and Equipment, flat with FY2026. None of the DOT materials, the text of S. 5572 or news coverage reviewed mentions separating the ATO from the FAA, replacing taxes with fees for air traffic services, or revenue bonds.

timeline.event: DOT announces a plan to build a new air traffic control system covering communications, surveillance, automation and facilities (telecommunications upgrades at over 4,600 sites, replacement of 618 radars, six new air traffic control centers and replacement of towers and approach control facilities). The release does not mention separating the Air Traffic Organization, user fees or governance changes.

Public Law 119-21 (H.R. 1) is enacted; its table of contents lists Sec. 40003, 'Air traffic control improvements,' and a White House fact sheet says the law provides $12.5 billion to modernize air traffic control systems, retire aging equipment, hire and train controllers and consolidate outdated facilities, without mentioning separation of the Air Traffic Organization or user fees. DOT calls the law the Working Families Tax Cut Act and, in a 2025-06-26 op-ed, called the $12.5 billion a down payment and said more money would be needed.

DOT releases its FY2027 budget request. The Budget Highlights request $4.0 billion for FAA Facilities and Equipment, flat with FY2026 (about $1.5 billion of it for the new air traffic control system), describe it as complementing the $12.5 billion provided in FY2025, and propose no reorganization of the air traffic organization and no new air traffic user fees (release date from DOT's budget page; the Highlights page was last updated 2026-05-05).

Senator Eric Schmitt introduces the Modern Skies Act as S. 5572, referred to the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee; it would appropriate $30.1 billion for FY2027: $10 billion for a pilot to modernize terminals at up to three transitional hub airports, $10.1 billion for FAA air traffic control improvements (including $7.2 billion for a common automation platform and controller workstation, $2 billion for cloud computing, $600 million for traffic flow management and $300 million to consolidate terminal facilities), and $10 billion for terminal air traffic control facilities and airport grants, and would allow transfers among the paragraphs of section 40003(a) of Public Law 119-21. The text does not mention an Air Traffic Organization separation, user fees, bonds or changes to FAA governance. No committee action was found. (Cite govinfo BILLS-119s5572is in place of the Senate-hosted draft.)

title: Restructure air traffic control: separate the ATO, change funding, modernize systems
uncertainties: Public Law 119-21 Sec. 40003 is confirmed from the law's table of contents and from S. 5572's reference to section 40003(a), but the statute text of Sec. 40003 (including the $12.5 billion amount) could not be read because the govinfo copy ends before Title IV, so the amount rests on FAA, White House and DOT material. The absence of any structural reform (ATO separation, user fees, revenue bonds) rests on S. 5572, DOT materials, Nextgov, FedScoop and AOPA coverage plus web searches; other congressional bills were not enumerated. Remote tower and center consolidation status was searched once and returned only 2021 to 2023 material. The FY2027 $4.0 billion Facilities and Equipment figure is from DOT's Budget Highlights; the statement that the Highlights propose no reorganization of the air traffic organization and no new user fee comes from a summary of the document, not a line-by-line read. An FAA fact sheet says about 20 billion dollars more is needed, a figure that differs from the $30.1 billion in S. 5572.
